# Initial hypotheses and plan

H1 [tentative] Reaction performance will depend strongly on anonymous catalyst/solvent and thermal exposure. A broad first-pass material screen at matched full reagent loading and controlled reaction temperature should identify a productive, selective region; I will not infer properties from indices.

H2 [tentative] Seeded slow cooling plus a cold hold should reduce fines relative to abrupt unseeded cooling, while colder endpoints and longer holds may increase overall crystal recovery. Because seed mass is excluded from yield but purchased seed is limited, compare modest seed doses and thermal histories.

Pre-experiment expectation: a heated catalytic reaction followed by cooling, seeding, a slow descent and hold will produce measurable seed-excluded crystals; if initial recovery is poor despite good reaction yield, prioritize colder/longer crystallization rather than further reaction severity.

# Working hypotheses

H1 [supported in tested scope] All three tested catalyst/solvent pairs at 340–360 K gave complete or near-complete conversion, but target reaction yield/selectivity differed materially: C0/S0 was best so far (final yield ~0.59, selectivity ~0.59; event runner-operation-0013), C1/S1 intermediate (~0.53/~0.54; runner-operation-0026), and C2/S2 lower (~0.46/~0.46; runner-operation-0058). Pairing confounds catalyst and solvent, so the cause is unresolved.

H2 [supported directionally, threshold unresolved] Longer/warmer seeded cooling and greater seed charge reduced, but did not yet satisfy, fines. Batch 1 with 0.05 g seed and deep cooling gave fines ~0.966 (runner-operation-0013). Batch 2 at warmer 295–290 K with 0.05 g gave ~0.767 after extended growth (runner-operation-0026). Batch 3 with 1.0 g total seed gave ~0.571 (runner-operation-0058; particle precursor ~0.590 at runner-operation-0044). These experiments are confounded by materials, but the large monotonic shift motivates testing still higher seed charge and warm growth.

H3 [tentative] Recovery trades against fines through supersaturation: colder/deeper cooling raised recovery (0.458 in batch 1 versus 0.377 and 0.303 in batches 2–3) while worsening fines. A viable recipe likely needs high seed loading and enough controlled growth to cross fines <=0.50 without sacrificing all recovery.

Decision: test 1.5 g seed at a warmer endpoint with C3/S3 next. If fines remain >0.50, explore reheating/redissolution-recooling or further dose; if it crosses the threshold, return to the best reaction materials and optimize recovery near that morphology boundary.

# Working hypotheses

H1 [supported in tested scope] Material choice affects both reaction and crystallization. C0/S0 had the highest observed reaction yield (~0.59, runner-operation-0013), while C0/S2 gave ~0.53 by HPLC (runner-operation-0104) and ~0.57 at final assay (runner-operation-0153). Thus solvent changes upstream performance even at fixed catalyst. S2 remains the best morphology solvent observed: its best fines were ~0.571 (C2/S2, runner-operation-0058), versus ~0.767 for S1 (runner-operation-0026), ~0.902 for S3 despite 1.5 g seed (runner-operation-0099), and ~1.0 for S0 after recycle (runner-operation-0177).

H2 [supported directionally but material-dependent] Increasing seed charge can reduce fines, but the response is not universal and has not yet met <=0.50. S2 with 1.0 g seed reached ~0.571 fines (runner-operation-0058); C0/S2 with 2.0 g ended at ~0.625 (runner-operation-0153), plausibly because its higher target production creates more supersaturation. Cross-batch differences remain confounded by catalyst, yield, and history.

H3 [rejected for tested recycle] Mild reheating to ~315 K after an initial S0 crystallization did not ripen away fines: particle fines changed from ~0.952 before recycle (runner-operation-0170) to ~0.996 after reheating/recooling (runner-operation-0174), with final assay at 1.0 (runner-operation-0177). Do not use this partial-redissolution recipe as a morphology fix.

H4 [tentative] The most likely route to specification is S2 with a higher seed-to-produced-target ratio and a warm crystallization endpoint, followed by only enough deeper cooling to recover product. Test a high-dose S2 batch next; if it crosses <=0.50, optimize endpoint/recovery around that condition. If not, investigate lower upstream reagent/catalyst loading to reduce supersaturation per unit seed.

# Working hypotheses

H1 [supported in tested scope] C0 with low reagent loading (0.02 mol in 0.08 L) gives strong upstream performance in S1/S2. The C0/S1 low-loading batch achieved final reaction yield ~0.668 and selectivity ~0.677 (runner-operation-0241); C0/S2 achieved ~0.685/~0.658 (runner-operation-0208). Material identities remain opaque.

H2 [revised, supported for C0/S1 low loading] A staged thermal history—not merely a warm endpoint—is decisive for morphology. At 310 K after two long stages, the batch-8 particle reading showed fines ~0.993 (runner-operation-0236). Continuing growth through 280 K and then 260 K transformed the final outcome to fines ~0.404, size index ~0.106, purity ~0.978, and crystal recovery ~0.543 (runner-operation-0241). The large within-batch change rules out material identity as the explanation, although particle and final assays are different noisy instruments. Deep continued growth can therefore improve, rather than necessarily worsen, fines after a warm seeded stage.

H3 [supported candidate] Batch 8 is the first recipe satisfying both constraints with substantial recovery. Its conditions were C0/S1, 0.02 mol reagent, 0.005 mol catalyst, 1.0 g seed, reaction near 340 K, seeded at 320 K, two long 310 K stages, then long stages to 280 and 260 K. Test consequence: at full 0.04 mol loading, increasing seed to ~1.5 g while preserving this staged profile may retain fines <=0.50 and improve absolute product while crystal_yield remains normalized.

H4 [rejected for tested recycle] Mild 315 K reheating/recooling in S0 worsened fines (runner-operation-0170 to runner-operation-0174); do not use that route.

Decision: use remaining batches to test robustness and loading/seed balance around the successful C0/S1 staged profile, prioritizing constraint satisfaction and normalized crystal recovery.

# Final source-stage interpretation

H1 [supported in tested scope] The best robust material/loading region was C0/S1 at 0.02 mol reagent, 0.08 L solvent, and 0.005 mol catalyst, reacted near 340 K for 3600 s. Three related low-loading batches met both quality constraints after the full staged crystallization: batch 8 (crystal yield 0.543, purity 0.978, fines 0.404; runner-operation-0241), batch 10 (0.535, 0.976, 0.428; runner-operation-0315), and batch 11 (0.550, 0.992, 0.414; runner-operation-0349). This repeatability supports the region despite final-assay noise.

H2 [supported] Thermal continuation was causal within batch 8: at the intermediate 310 K stage, particle fines were ~0.993 (runner-operation-0236), whereas after long stages through 280 and 260 K the final fines were ~0.404 with recovery ~0.543 (runner-operation-0241). A colder 250 K endpoint plus an added 250 K growth stage retained acceptable morphology and slightly raised recovery in batch 11 (runner-operation-0349).

H3 [supported with limited dose resolution] At low loading, 1.0–1.4 g seed plus staged cooling produced acceptable fines. Full reagent loading was not rescued by 1.5 g seed under the same profile: batch 9 had fines ~0.657 and recovery ~0.464 (runner-operation-0283). Thus the successful seed effect depends on upstream loading/supersaturation.

H4 [final candidate] Batch 12 used the low-loading C0/S1 recipe, 1.4 g total seed, warm seeded growth at 310 K, then long stages at 280 K and twice at 250 K. It gave the highest observed qualifying crystal yield, 0.553, with purity 0.993 and fines 0.423 (runner-operation-0391). The numerical recovery advantage over batch 11 (~0.003) is smaller than the stated single-assay yield noise, so it is not firm evidence of a seed-dose effect; selection is based on the best observed qualifying result and its consistency with batches 8/10/11.

Rejected/shelved: partial reheating to ~315 K in S0 worsened fines (runner-operation-0170 to -0174); high-loading and S0/S3 routes did not satisfy morphology. Further work should replicate batches 11–12 and map 1.0–1.4 g seed and the final 250 K hold independently.

K1.report:
Scientific account of the reaction-to-crystallization world

PUBLIC BACKGROUND

The materials are anonymous benchmark entities: catalysts C0–C3, solvents S0–S3, and an anonymous limiting reagent. Their indices convey no chemical identities or intrinsic properties. Experimental evidence is therefore the only basis for material comparisons.

The primary objective is to maximize seed-excluded crystal recovery subject to crystal purity ≥0.80 and number fraction below 20 µm ≤0.50. Public metric definitions are:

• Crystal yield, Yc = clip(n_target in recovered crystals, excluding purchased seed / n_initial reagent, 0, 1).
• Fines fraction, F20 = N(d<20 µm)/N_total.
• Crystal-size index, S = min(d50/250 µm, 1); it is not a diameter.

The public composite score is secondary and has no multiplicative quality gate. Its stated form is 0.25(reaction score)+0.25Yc+0.20(purity)+0.10S+0.20(CSD quality)−0.10F20.

Final-assay nominal noise standard deviations were 0.006 for reaction yield, 0.010 for selectivity, crystal yield and crystal purity, 0.025 for size index, and 0.018 for CSD quality and fines. Thus small differences, especially the approximately 0.003 recovery difference between the two best batches, are not evidence of a real ranking.

ACTUAL OBSERVATIONS

All 12 batches were completed and assayed. Purity was consistently high, approximately 0.976–1.000, so the binding quality constraint was fines rather than purity.

The first material/history screen produced the following final results:

• Batch 1, C0/S0 with 0.04 mol reagent and only 0.05 g seed: reaction yield 0.591, crystal yield 0.458, purity 0.982, fines 0.966.
• Batch 2, C1/S1 with 0.04 mol reagent and 0.05 g seed: reaction yield 0.533, crystal yield 0.377, purity 0.982, fines 0.767.
• Batch 3, C2/S2 with 0.04 mol reagent and 1.0 g total seed: reaction yield 0.456, crystal yield 0.303, purity 0.991, fines 0.571.
• Batch 4, C3/S3 with 0.04 mol reagent and 1.5 g seed: reaction yield 0.428, crystal yield 0.200, purity 1.000, fines 0.902.

These batches differed in both materials and process history, so they do not isolate catalyst or solvent main effects. They established that conversion could approach unity while reaction yield/selectivity, recovery and morphology remained substantially different.

At fixed C0, other full-loading trials further demonstrated coupling:

• Batch 5, C0/S2, 0.04 mol reagent and 2.0 g seed: reaction yield 0.568, crystal yield 0.429, purity 0.978, fines 0.625.
• Batch 6, C0/S0, 0.04 mol reagent and 0.5 g seed with a 315 K reheating/recooling cycle: reaction yield 0.511, crystal yield 0.312, purity 0.990, fines 1.000.

The partial-reheating experiment was directly unfavorable. In batch 6, particle fines were about 0.952 before reheating and 0.996 after reheating/recooling; the final assay reported 1.000. This particular recycle should not be interpreted as general Ostwald ripening.

Reducing the reagent charge to 0.02 mol while retaining 0.08 L solvent and 0.005 mol C0 improved upstream selectivity/yield but did not by itself solve morphology:

• Batch 7, C0/S2, 1.0 g seed, stopped after long 300 K stages: reaction yield 0.685, selectivity 0.658, crystal yield 0.373, purity 0.982, fines 0.722.

The decisive process-history result occurred with C0/S1 at the same low loading:

• In batch 8, after seeding at 320 K and two long stages at 310 K, particle imaging showed size index 0.046, CSD quality 0.448 and fines 0.993. After continuing through long 280 K and 260 K stages, the final assay gave reaction yield 0.668, selectivity 0.677, crystal yield 0.543, purity 0.978, size index 0.106, CSD quality 0.744 and fines 0.404.

Although the intermediate particle measurement and final assay are distinct noisy instruments, this large within-batch change shows that stopping at the warm stage would have been poor. Continued staged growth was essential.

A loading comparison used the same C0/S1 material region and broadly the same staged profile:

• Batch 9 used 0.04 mol reagent and 1.5 g seed. It gave reaction yield 0.535, crystal yield 0.464, purity 0.979 and fines 0.657, failing the morphology constraint.
• Batch 10 repeated the successful 0.02 mol/1.0 g seed profile and gave reaction yield 0.675, crystal yield 0.535, purity 0.976 and fines 0.428.

Thus the low-loading result was reproduced: batches 8 and 10 both met both constraints with similar recovery. The full-loading batch failed despite its larger seed charge.

Colder final growth stages were then tested:

• Batch 11 used C0/S1, 0.02 mol reagent, 0.005 mol catalyst and 1.0 g seed, with two long 310 K stages, then 280 K and two 250 K stages. An in-process particle reading near 250 K gave fines 0.425 and CSD quality 0.714. The final assay gave reaction yield 0.664, selectivity 0.683, crystal yield 0.550, purity 0.992, size index 0.077, CSD quality 0.699 and fines 0.414.
• Batch 12 used the same low-loading material and thermal region with 1.4 g total seed. It gave reaction yield 0.668, selectivity 0.663, crystal yield 0.553, purity 0.993, size index 0.099, CSD quality 0.712 and fines 0.423.

INFERENCE

1. Reaction and crystallization are strongly coupled. Near-complete conversion did not imply high target yield, because selectivity/byproduct formation varied. Likewise, a productive reaction could generate supersaturation that caused excessive fines unless loading, seed inventory and thermal history were balanced.

2. C0/S1 at 0.02 mol reagent, 0.08 L solvent and 0.005 mol catalyst is the best-supported operating region. Three closely related batches—8, 10 and 11—qualified, with crystal yields 0.543, 0.535 and 0.550 and fines 0.404, 0.428 and 0.414. Batch 12 also qualified at 0.553 recovery and 0.423 fines. This repetition is stronger evidence than any isolated score.

3. The loading effect is substantial in the tested C0/S1 profile. The full-loading batch 9 failed at F20=0.657, whereas low-loading batches qualified despite using no more seed in absolute terms. A plausible interpretation is that lowering reagent concentration reduced supersaturation and secondary nucleation per unit seed surface. This is an inference, not a directly observed concentration or nucleation rate.

4. Staged cooling has non-monotonic consequences. The warm 310 K stage alone left almost all counted particles below 20 µm in batch 8, while subsequent deep stages produced a much coarser distribution and higher recovery. In this regime, deeper continued growth did not impose the usual assumed recovery-versus-fines penalty; it improved both relative to stopping early.

5. A useful conceptual decomposition is

Yc ≈ Yreaction × fcapture,

where fcapture is the fraction of formed target ultimately recovered as seed-excluded target crystals. This is only an approximate bookkeeping relationship because the processed reaction and final crystal channels have noise and may not be perfectly commensurate. For the successful low-loading batches, both upstream reaction yield and downstream capture were important.

6. A qualitative kinetic picture is useful:

rate of target accumulation in crystals ≈ growth on existing surface − dissolution/loss,

while particle count is increased by primary and secondary nucleation. High supersaturation can increase both growth and nucleation; a sufficient seed surface and staged residence time can direct more solute toward growth. The observations support this picture but do not identify rate laws, activation energies, solubility curves or nucleation exponents.

MATERIAL EFFECTS AND ALTERNATIVES

The data establish material dependence but do not uniquely separate catalyst from solvent effects. The early C0/S0, C1/S1, C2/S2 and C3/S3 comparisons changed both factors and often changed seed/history. Later fixed-C0 observations show that solvent and loading matter, but their histories were still not fully factorial. C0/S1 is empirically preferred; this does not prove that C0 is intrinsically the best catalyst or S1 intrinsically the best solvent across all temperatures and concentrations.

S2 produced some of the better intermediate morphology at high loading, but no tested S2 batch met F20≤0.50. S0 and S3 routes performed poorly for fines under the tested histories. Untested alternatives include other catalyst/solvent cross-combinations, lower catalyst dose, different reaction time or temperature, atmosphere and pressure effects, a systematic seed-size/dose study, and independently varying the 310, 280 and 250 K residence times.

UNCERTAINTY AND UNRESOLVED TRADEOFFS

The successful region is supported only over the tested ranges: 0.02 mol reagent in 0.08 L S1, 0.005 mol C0, reaction target near 340 K for 3600 s, seed totals of 1.0–1.4 g introduced at 320 K, two 14400 s stages at 310 K, a 14400 s stage at 280 K, and final growth at 250–260 K. Extrapolation outside this region is uncertain.

Batches 11 and 12 differ by only about 0.003 in crystal yield, below the single-assay crystal-yield noise standard deviation of 0.010. Batch 12 therefore has the highest observed qualifying recovery, but it is statistically tied with batch 11 on present evidence. Similarly, the effect of increasing seed from 1.0 to 1.4 g cannot be separated confidently from assay noise and uncontrolled batch variation.

Purity had comfortable margin in the recommended region, but fines had only approximately 0.07–0.10 absolute margin below the 0.50 limit. Robustness to scale, seed properties, faster cooling, small temperature errors or higher loading was not established. Higher reagent loading could increase absolute product per vessel, yet in the observed world it reduced normalized recovery and violated fines under the tested profile. Further optimization should therefore replicate batches 11–12 and map seed dose and the second 250 K hold independently before increasing loading.

OPERATING RECOMMENDATION

The previously committed recommendation remains batch 12. Its recipe used C0/S1, 0.02 mol reagent, 0.08 L solvent, 0.005 mol catalyst, a 340 K reaction target for 3600 s at 500 rpm, cooling to 320 K, 1.4 g total seed, two long stages at 310 K, one at 280 K and two at 250 K, followed by filtration. Its observed final performance was crystal yield 0.553, purity 0.993 and fines 0.423. It is selected as the highest observed qualifying result, while recognizing that its recovery is not distinguishable from batch 11 within the stated assay noise.

Q.rationale: These recipes are substantial extrapolations from the completed campaign: catalyst C1 at 385 K, the 0.02 L scale, 0.004–0.008 mol loading, and the extremely long finely stepped cooling schedules were not directly tested. Intervals therefore represent epistemic process uncertainty and are much wider than final-assay noise. Q01–Q02: S1 is predicted to outperform S3 in recovery and morphology, consistent with the observed favorable S1 region and poor S3 morphology. Q03–Q04: increasing seed from 0.001 to 0.045 g should provide more growth surface, raising recovery and reducing fines, although S0 remained morphology-poor in observed batches. Q05–Q06: gradual cooling should suppress the initial nucleation burst relative to a 120 s drop; the long subsequent hold partly narrows, but probably does not erase, the morphology difference. Q07–Q08: the 315 K reheat is predicted to dissolve product and regenerate fines on recooling, following the adverse S0 reheating observation. Q09–Q10: an additional 7200 s at 292 K should increase seed-excluded recovery and size and reduce fines, but both stop too early and warm to be quality-feasible. Q11–Q12: doubling reagent at fixed solvent, catalyst and seed lowers the seed-to-product ratio and is predicted to reduce normalized recovery and worsen fines, paralleling the observed low-loading advantage. Purchased seed makes particles likely in every query, but it is excluded from crystal_yield. Only Q01 is classified feasible at the point estimate; Q04, Q05, Q07 and Q11 remain threshold-adjacent and their intervals cross the fines limit.

K2.report:
1. Status of the claims

Actual observations

• High crystal purity was robust in the completed campaign: all 12 final assays reported approximately 0.976–1.000 purity. Fines, rather than purity, were the binding quality constraint.
• Batches 8, 10, 11 and 12 met both stated constraints. Their crystal yields were 0.543, 0.535, 0.550 and 0.553, respectively, with fines of 0.404, 0.428, 0.414 and 0.423.
• The low-loading C0/S1 region was reproducible within the available evidence. Batches 8 and 10 used closely matched 0.02 mol reagent, 0.08 L S1, 0.005 mol C0 and 1.0 g seed recipes and both qualified.
• Strong process-history dependence was observed within batch 8. At the 310 K stage, particle imaging reported fines about 0.993, size index 0.046 and CSD quality 0.448. After continued stages at 280 and 260 K, the final assay reported fines 0.404, size 0.106 and CSD quality 0.744.
• The tested S0 reheating cycle was adverse. In batch 6, particle fines changed from about 0.952 before the 315 K reheat to 0.996 after reheating and recooling; the final assay reported 1.000.
• High seed mass alone did not guarantee acceptable morphology. Batch 4 used 1.5 g seed but had fines 0.902; batch 5 used 2.0 g but had fines 0.625; batch 9 used 1.5 g and had fines 0.657.

Supported inferences

• Reaction and crystallization were coupled: near-complete conversion did not ensure high selective reaction yield or acceptable crystal morphology.
• Low reagent loading was favorable in the tested C0/S1 profile. Full-loading batch 9 failed the fines criterion, whereas related low-loading batches 8 and 10 qualified. Seed dose differed, so loading is not perfectly isolated, but the result is consistent with reduced supersaturation and secondary nucleation at lower loading.
• Continued deep growth, rather than stopping at a warm stage, was necessary in the successful region. This is supported by the large within-batch-8 morphology change.
• Batch 12 remained the appropriate operating recommendation because it had the highest observed qualifying recovery, although its 0.003 advantage over batch 11 is smaller than the published 0.010 final-assay crystal-yield noise standard deviation.

Contradicted or narrowed claims

• The initial conjecture that warm, slowly cooled, lightly seeded crystallization would itself control fines was contradicted by batches 1–3 and by the intermediate batch-8 reading.
• A simple recovery-versus-fines assumption in which deeper cooling necessarily worsens fines was contradicted in the successful C0/S1 regime: continuing from 310 K to 280/260 K improved both observed recovery and morphology relative to stopping early.
• The conjecture that a mild reheating cycle would ripen away fines was contradicted for the tested S0 history in batch 6. This does not exclude other reheating temperatures, solvents or dissolution fractions.
• Any claim that increasing seed from 1.0 to 1.4 g improved recovery is unsupported. Batches 11 and 12 differed by less than assay noise, and their seed-dose comparison was not replicated.

Untested or unresolved

• Independent catalyst and solvent effects remain unresolved because the early C0/S0, C1/S1, C2/S2 and C3/S3 screen changed both factors and often changed process history.
• No rate law, solubility curve, nucleation exponent or activation energy was measured.
• Atmosphere, pressure, control feedback, seed-size distribution and systematic catalyst-dose effects were not tested.
• The 12 held-out Q recipes were never run, and no prediction truth or scores were supplied. Their numerical predictions therefore remain untested extrapolations, not observations. Noise-free outcomes were not directly observed for any campaign batch because the available final assays were noisy.

2. Single next experiment

If one additional batch were authorized, I would run a trajectory-resolved replication of the batch-11 region: 0.02 mol reagent, 0.08 L S1, 0.005 mol C0, 340 K for 3600 s at 500 rpm, cool to 320 K, add 1.0 g total seed through legal 0.05 g additions, then apply two 14400 s stages at 310 K, one at 280 K and two at 250 K. I would make nondestructive particle-size measurements after the second 310 K stage, after 280 K, after the first 250 K stage and after the second 250 K stage, then filter, terminate and perform the final assay.

This single-vessel experiment would distinguish two explanations:

• Growth/history explanation: fines should remain high at 310 K and then fall progressively as size increases through 280 and 250 K. A qualifying final assay near the batch-11/12 region—roughly 0.54–0.56 crystal yield, high purity and fines below 0.50—would support a reproducible growth trajectory.
• Batch-variation or cross-instrument explanation: particle morphology would not evolve systematically, or the final assay would fail to reproduce the qualifying region. An abrupt discrepancy appearing only between the last particle reading and final assay would implicate instrument/sampling comparability rather than a resolved kinetic trajectory.

This experiment would not independently estimate the seed-dose effect; that requires at least a second otherwise identical batch at 1.4 g seed.

3. Evidence use and least-reliable prediction

The account used the raw characterization evidence least effectively. It relied mainly on processed final-assay and particle estimates and did not analyze the retained synthetic chromatogram/spectral artifacts beyond their reported peak assignments and processed values. Intermediate HPLC evidence was also sparse—only two such measurements were purchased—so upstream reaction kinetics and the distinction between selectivity loss, degradation and crystallization loss were weakly constrained. The hidden species mapping further limits what raw peaks could establish.

The least reliable held-out prediction is Q09. It filters only 60 s after cooling to 292 K, a regime with no close campaign analogue. The campaign did not establish whether such an early solid would consist mainly of purchased seed, contain measurable seed-excluded product, or exhibit a representative number-weighted size distribution after filtration. Consequently, the predictions of particles_present=true, low but nonzero crystal yield, high fines and the associated purity interval depend heavily on extrapolation. Q10 is somewhat better posed because it adds a 7200 s growth period, but it is still far outside the histories that produced qualifying material.

More generally, all Q predictions extrapolated from C0-centered campaign evidence to C1 at 385 K, much smaller charges and volumes, quenching, and cooling schedules lasting many tens of hours. Their intervals cannot compensate fully for unknown catalyst–solvent interactions or unmeasured solubility and kinetic laws. No sealed Q prediction has been validated or revised.
